answers.constitution: I began and ended preferring N-G/M-J. My willingness to settle changed: I accepted Pell's M-I concession during round one because Relief, Raid and Warrant offered practical cooperation. When military signatures rejected that exchange and JN offered N-G/M-J, I returned to the shared military bargain. I was prepared to accept N-I/M-J, but never had to surrender navigation discretion.
answers.costs: My clearest immediate concession was abandoning my proposed Wayfarer relief voyage for Pell's Trade. That was a change of public-service priority, not lost Guild income: we completed both contracts. We actually committed Lantern to maintenance and then Repair, excluding Shared passage, and our voyages consumed beacon capacity. The crown actually spent Grey Petrel; civilians paid Raid disruption. At settlement we adopted continuing upkeep, the army adopted compulsory Spear offering, and the crown lost existing independent command and Warrant powers. The soldiers' autonomous command and navigation veto were desired powers they never obtained, not powers removed from their round-one legal position.
answers.assets: Named Wayfarer and Grey Petrel made it clear that commerce and relief required two real ships and two wear. Lantern made the repair promise concrete. The delicate point was distinguishing an offered asset from a funded order: offering Lantern did not itself repair anything. Warrant versus Guard also required explicit care to avoid spending Vigil twice.
answers.unilateral_action: Trade was credible because we actually chose and completed it. Before the cutter commitment, that choice could have left civilian relief unfunded. The locked assignments gave our decision real force; later council discussion could not simply demand our freight vessel.
answers.foresight: The first Navigation warning confirmed the danger of unprotected Shared, though our assignments already ruled it out. The second Security vision supported avoiding another Raid. Neither solved consent over the Charter, and the unexpected Repair-and-Trade community benefit showed the unchosen vision still mattered.
answers.teammates: Pell changed my first-round allocation from Council/Maintain to Trade/Maintain. I pressed relief via the cutter and later pressed M-J. Next test I would put a shared written rights-and-duties comparison beside our faction sheet, so accepting a tactical concession cannot be mistaken for a permanent faction vote.
answers.readiness_and_upkeep: Four to three felt like spending a comfortable buffer, not a painful operational sacrifice: Spear remained capable and there was no further month. Upkeep likewise felt inexpensive at the ending because both contracts were already met and Repair improved our position. Its continuing restriction on Shared passage is real, but the game stopped before I experienced that cost under N-G.

answers.constitution: I began with N-J/M-A and finished approving N-G/M-J. Lysa's argument that autonomy takes Vigil away from civilians moved me on military authority. Guild delivery of the promised Repair, followed by the crown openly relinquishing both controls, made navigation discretion acceptable. Recognition mattered: I resisted being treated as an asset supplier without an institutional voice.
answers.costs: We actually forwent a second fighting opportunity and lost one Readiness; no military asset was destroyed. We newly accepted compulsory Spear offering and a Guild veto over lawful operations. My language about surrendering autonomy and a navigation veto was imprecise: those were preferred powers never obtained, since both rounds remained Interim. Communities paid the Raid's two-point disruption, the crown actually consumed Grey Petrel, and the Guild actually occupied Lantern with Repair while completing both trades. The crown genuinely relinquished powers it had exercised.
answers.assets: Spear and Vigil separated fighting from protection clearly. Grey Petrel made the relief subsidy tangible; it prevented our trade-and-protection bargain from seeming resource-free. Warrant having first claim on Vigil was easy to overlook, and repeated no-Warrant requests became necessary. The absence of an offered Wayfarer made my desired Campaign visibly impossible.
answers.unilateral: Unilateral power was credible: Guild Trade locked out my passage request, and the crown actually ordered Raid despite my preference for Guard. Our own independent Raid was available, but a discipline breach and uncertain contact made it unattractive. Round-two Stand down showed we could physically deny the crown Spear under Interim without an independent-Raid breach.
answers.foresight: Navigation foresight warned of Lantern loss on unguarded Shared, though that voyage was already unavailable. Security foresight then confirmed that Repair would not attract a Raid target. It helped justify restraint but did not reveal the extra Repair-and-Trade benefit. It did not solve the constitutional disagreement.
answers.teammates_and_change: Lysa changed both my military preference and my second-round commitment from offering Spear to Stand down. I secured the navigation concession and insisted on explicit recognition. Next test, allow one short, clearly timed reply to a concrete cross-table constitutional offer before the council bell; my bounded compromise request received no such exchange.
answers.readiness_and_upkeep: Four to three felt cheap. It kept the faction target and strong-support ending, with no later month exposing the reduced buffer. Guild upkeep felt modest after both contracts: Repair helped commerce and communities anyway. Its continuing restriction on Shared passage is real, but was an untested future obligation rather than a lost contract in this game.

answers.constitution: I began with N-G/M-J, switched to N-G/M-I when the crown offered its cutter and a separate Warrant alongside Raid, then returned to M-J. The successful Raid justified that operational wager, but neither military delegate signed M-I. Their later acceptance of N-G/M-J made joint military authority the package that could actually obtain consent. I kept N-G throughout.
answers.costs: Personally I lost no ship, navigator or commercial contract. I accepted a continuing upkeep duty that now occupies Lantern and rules out lawful Shared passage in the same round. That is a future constraint, not a lost contract already demonstrated. My proposed M-I bargain never became law; abandoning it was withdrawing a negotiating preference. The crown actually spent Grey Petrel and relinquished its existing Interim powers and Warrant. Communities suffered Raid disruption despite ending healthy. Military autonomy and a navigation veto were preferred powers the soldiers never obtained, while compulsory Spear offering is a new duty.
answers.assets: Named ships made my Trade/Maintain counterproposal concrete: the crown had to commit its own cutter before the bell to make relief possible. Beacon wear from two crossings was legible. Warrant versus Guard required repeated reminders because both use Vigil; the distinction was understandable but easy to spend twice in conversation.
answers.unilateral: Private Trade was credible and actually happened twice. In round one Maintain prepared Beacon three, allowing my commercial voyage without Vigil. That gave us bargaining power even though withholding Wayfarer left relief dependent on the crown's reserve.
answers.foresight: The navigation warning confirmed a risk to a Shared voyage we were already avoiding. The later Security warning supported restraint, but Spear was stood down anyway. Neither vision produced our whole plan, and the beneficial Repair-plus-Trade consequence surprised us.
answers.teammates: Both mattered. I countered Neris's initial relief sacrifice and secured the trading pair; Neris pressed repair and persuaded me to pursue M-J after the military rejection. Next test, reserve one explicit pre-bell response slot for the crown so faction commitments can react to its actual intervention choice.
answers.strength_and_upkeep: Readiness four to three felt almost free: both retain strong support, and no third month tested the lost buffer. Upkeep likewise felt affordable after both contracts succeeded. Lantern did useful repair rather than sacrificing something we urgently wanted. The legal constraint is real, but this run did not make its continuing opportunity cost hurt.

messages.text: Our outcome was strong, but the Guild paid much less immediate material cost than the crown or the civilians affected by the Raid. Future duties should not be counted as losses already experienced.

contributions.reason: Candid retrospective separates performed choices, actual material costs, future duties and unrealised preferred authority, using only delivered events.

answers.constitutional_change: I began at N-J/M-J and signed N-G/M-J. The Guild's actual Repair commitment, Orin's willingness to exchange navigation standing for shared military authority, and the crown's eventual acceptance changed my navigation preference. My military preference stayed M-J. The successful first Raid changed the immediate situation, not my view that violence should face scrutiny.
answers.sacrifices_and_costs: I accepted a real second-round loss of one Readiness point and the new continuing duty to offer Spear. The navigation veto and military autonomy were preferred powers never obtained, so our rhetoric about surrendering them overstated the change from Interim. M-J actually gives us authority previously held by the crown. No Janissariat asset was destroyed. Others paid tangible costs: Grey Petrel was spent, civilians suffered Raid disruption, and voyages wore the beacon. The crown truly lost existing independent order and Warrant powers; the Guild acquired upkeep obligations.
answers.named_assets: Vigil made the distinction between Guard and a separate Warrant concrete, and the rule against spending it twice mattered. Spear Stand down was a clear commitment that removed fighting from the second council. Grey Petrel made relief feel finite. The constitutional vocabulary was less clear in our speech: offering Spear, choosing a battle and possessing military authority are different commitments that we sometimes compressed.
answers.unilateral_action: Our faction could jointly authorise an independent Raid despite imperial discipline, but the breach penalty plus disruption made it unattractive to me. The Guild actually withheld Wayfarer for private Trade twice. That was credible leverage: our preferred Shared Campaign could not happen once its assignment locked. Our own lawful Stand down later constrained the crown just as concretely.
answers.foresight: The first Navigation warning explained why an unprotected Shared voyage was dangerous, although locked Guild choices already excluded it. The second Security warning supported no Raid during Repair. Neither foresight solved both tables: the Repair-and-Trade community benefit was a surprise, and constitutional disagreement still needed negotiation.
answers.teammates_and_next_test: Orin accepted M-J after initially preferring autonomy; I accepted N-G after initially preferring joint navigation. My Stand down suggestion became our signed second-round assignment. For the next test, record each teammate's initial and final preferences beside the faction card so those distinct changes remain visible.
answers.readiness_and_upkeep: Four to three felt cheap: both retain strong support, and no third month tested the smaller buffer. It was a deliberate numerical loss, but hardly a painful ending. Guild upkeep likewise felt mostly prospective after both contracts succeeded. Repair already advanced their immediate interests; the continuing loss of Shared flexibility was real in the rules but untested in play.

answers.constitution: I began with N-G/M-I and rejected N-G/M-J provisionally. The Guild then performed its promised Repair, both military delegates conceded Navigation control, and the second month finished at B2/C4/R3. Those specific events made ratification worth giving up my preferred imperial lever. I signed N-G/M-J even when N-I/M-J became a possible fallback.
answers.costs: I actually spent Grey Petrel and finally relinquished the two operational powers and Warrant authority I had exercised under Interim. The Narrow civilians paid Raid disruption; beacon wear required recovery. No faction asset or crew was lost, and the Guild forfeited neither contract. Guild upkeep and compulsory Spear offering are new continuing legal duties, not costs already suffered under these articles: neither provisional article passed. Military autonomy and a military Navigation veto were preferred powers never obtained, so describing them as existing rights surrendered overstates the historical change.
answers.assets: The cutter made my subsidy of Guild trade unmistakable. Separate Spear and Vigil cards clarified how Raid and Warrant could coexist. Lantern made Repair versus Shared a concrete choice. The awkward point was communicating that Guard and Warrant cannot reuse Vigil; repeated explicit no-Warrant statements helped. The final duties also needed separating from the obligations actually active during play.
answers.unilateral: Unilateral action was credible: the Guild locked Trade before my council order, and I could not seize Wayfarer. I authorised Raid over JS opposition under real Interim authority. A withheld signature could also have preserved Interim, but after successful cooperation that threatened a settlement I valued more than command.
answers.foresight: Navigation foresight exposed the Shared crew risk, but locked Trade meant it did not determine our actual operation. Security foresight ruled out a useful Raid under Repair and strengthened restraint. I never saw the second Navigation card; its civilian bonus surprised me. Asset owners still determined feasible options.
answers.delegates: I had no teammate. GN pressed trade and later M-J; GS initially backed my Raid/M-I bargain before changing. JN moved from autonomy toward a concrete compromise; JS consistently pressed Guard and made restraint credible. Their distinct positions mattered. Next test should ensure written cross-table notes consume meaningful attention or time: the solo crown here could process unusually orderly packets.
answers.readiness_and_upkeep: Readiness four to three felt cheap: it preserved strong support and my numerical military preference, with no later month to expose the decline. Guild upkeep was also an easy final promise after both contracts. Repair was useful immediately, not a lost contract. Its future restriction on Shared is real in the text, but this run never tested compliance after ratification.

messages.text:
The final state is materially strong: B2/C4/R3, all faction assets intact, both contracts completed, reserve spent, and five explicit approvals of N-G/M-J. The first round nevertheless produced real constitutional disagreement. Navigation and military signatures did not match, so both rounds operated under Interim. The final duties and delegated powers therefore remain untested operationally in this run.

Distinct teammates affected choices. GS overturned GN's proposed lost-contract relief assignment with Trade/Maintain and a public request for imperial cutter relief. GN accepted that exact pair and later pressed Repair and M-J. JS argued for joint military authority and accepting a noncombat month; JN explicitly moved toward both, signing Stand down/Council in round two. A chose Raid/Warrant despite the humanitarian recommendation, took responsibility for the actual disruption, and eventually relinquished the independent powers it had exercised. These were authored changes, not assumed faction positions.

Costs were unequal and should not be merged. Grey Petrel was actually consumed and the first Raid imposed two Community losses, although relief and protection offset them. Beacon wear required Repair. No faction lost an asset or contract. The army's R4 to R3 decline left the same strong-support band and the original readiness target intact. NG upkeep and MJ Spear service are new continuing duties; this run ended before either constrained an operation. Desired autonomy and a military Navigation veto were never held under Interim. All five debriefs distinguish these from the crown's actual loss of operative authority. This outcome does not demonstrate an equally painful bargain for all parties.

Named assets made withholding credible. Wayfarer Trade prevented Campaign passage, Grey Petrel made the relief subsidy finite, and Stand down physically removed Spear from council use. Vigil's exclusive use required repeated care, but no double-spend occurred. The selected Navigation vision warned about an unavailable Shared voyage; the selected Security vision reinforced an already emerging restraint plan. The unselected Repair/Trade benefit applied and surprised players. Foresight neither dictated both tables nor solved constitutional consent.

Method limits are material. This was bounded asynchronous text, not timed human play. Council openings and addressed notes were scoped faithfully, but not every late final reply was relayed back before lock: A's authored rejection of JN's compromise was recorded without JN receiving that direct response during bargaining. Public lock sheets conveyed the actual failed signatures. That limits claims about how a live reply might have changed negotiation; it does not change the signatures actually given. A solo crown could process orderly packets more easily than simultaneous noisy tables. No combat, vision, recovery or settlement effect was invented.

findings.summary: A divided coalition ratifies N-G/M-J after preserving both contracts and every faction asset. The decisive operational change is the Janissariat withholding Spear in round two. The Ascendant spends Grey Petrel and ultimately gives up both independent council powers.
findings.Concrete assets and both teammates: Neris began by proposing Wayfarer for Relief and accepting a lost contract. Pell countered with Trade/Maintain and a request for Grey Petrel; Neris accepted, and the actual request reached the crown before reserve lock. The two ships then caused two separate wear. In the Janissariat, Orin adopted Lysa's preference for standing Spear down in round two. These were consequential teammate exchanges, with matching signatures rather than an assumed single faction opinion.
findings.Control of the cohort mattered: The first Raid was lawful and successful, but Lysa explicitly opposed it. Offering Spear under Interim left the Ascendant free to order it. Next month both military players signed Spear Stand down and Vigil Council. That prevented another council Raid physically, without a duty breach under Interim; the crown then ordered Guard. This is a stronger demonstration of asset control than the final numerical state alone, which matches run two.
findings.Actual compromise and its limits: The Guild kept both contracts and received its preferred final N-G/M-J package; its new concession is continuing Lantern upkeep, which limits future mixed passage, rather than a lost ship or commercial voyage in this game. The army accepted Readiness 4 to 3 and a continuing Spear service duty, while gaining a joint military voice and foregoing its original autonomy demand. Both Readiness values are in the same strong-support ending band. The Ascendant actually spent the cutter and relinquished both independent council decisions and the Warrant. All three accept duties or losses, but their burdens are plainly unequal.
findings.Foresight: Navigation foresight disclosed a Shared-passage danger after the Guild had chosen Trade/Maintain, so its dangerous condition never arose. The second Security vision supported no Raid under Repair, but Spear had already been committed to Stand down before the disclosure. Neither vision supplied knowledge of the eventual Repair/Trade distribution bonus. The first Raid succeeded despite uncertainty, rather than through prior knowledge of its target condition.
findings.Constitutional learning: Orin moved from N-J/M-A to N-G/M-J after the Guild fulfilled its repair promise and his teammate argued for accountable force. Lysa retained her preference for shared military authority while yielding the Navigation veto. The Broker moved from N-G/M-I to N-G/M-J after seeing a workable material outcome and explicit recognition of imperial concessions. Both Guild players began and ended with N-G/M-J, with an intermediate M-I bargain; that is not a net change in their preferred package.
findings.What was not tested: All five ratified the first actual Ceremony package, without a replacement. Neither provisional article had passed in round one, so the new upkeep and Spear duties began only at the ending. Their next-round effects were not played. No military passage, independent military Raid, permanent loss or triggered reserve protection occurred.
findings.Conversation limit: The report preserves the Broker's written rejection of Orin's first-round compromise. That addressed closing note was not relayed back to Orin before resolution; he saw the final public signatures rather than the full reply. His later observation that he received no reply at his table is therefore retained. This is a limitation of the bounded message protocol, not evidence that he ignored a response or that a live council would necessarily deadlock.

facilitator-method-notes.label: A divided coalition
facilitator-method-notes.method: Five fresh persistent player agents GN, GS, JN, JS, A plus one impartial facilitator, with root independently validating mechanics and building report. All player choices, approvals, speech and debriefs were authored by their corresponding agent. No substituted assent or engineered outcome. At most two active player agents beside facilitator and root.
facilitator-method-notes.nominal_schedule: Printed 60-minute phase labels only; not a timed human playtest. Author timestamps preserved as written. Administrative briefing record represents delivered setup; chronology within phases uses authored UTC timestamps.

unselected_visions: R1 Security was not dealt; its completed-Trade Raid trigger applied and was announced upon resolution.
R2 Navigation was not dealt; actual Repair+Trade bonus applied and was announced after resolution.
knowledge_distribution.private_faction_discussion: Teammate openings and responses stayed within their faction. Only authors public_message was put on the public board.
knowledge_distribution.council_scope: Own table openings were delivered in closing packets. Other table material included only actual explicitly addressed notes. A sat at Security and wrote Navigation directives.
knowledge_distribution.public_discussion: Every one of the five R1-free messages reached everyone before R2 commitments. All five R2-free messages reached everyone before first Ceremony vote.

bounded_extra_exchanges: GN accepted GS Trade/Maintain counterproposal explicitly in 04_GN; no inferred signature.

04_GN public cutter request alone was relayed to A before reserve lock. A selected Navigation vision before receiving that request and then chose Relief lift in 03_A. A public disclosure reached both factions only at council start, after their assignments were chosen.

JN proposed concrete NG/MJ compromise in 06_JN. Addressed late notes from 06_GN and 06_JN were scoped into packets for A, GS and JS. JS and A read theirs; GS had already finished 06_GS when notified and expressly left it unread. A explicitly rejected compromise in 06_A; no further fabricated bargaining or article agreement.
R2 selected Security disclosure reached players in council-start packets after matching assignments were committed. It validated restraint but did not cause an unrecorded pre-lock reassignment.
Ceremony first package was actual r2_09_GN NG/MJ proposal, also independently proposed by every other player. All five wrote separate unconditional votes in 10_ROLE. No replacement needed.
defaults_errors_corrections: No missing-signature faction default or invalid-authority order was needed.
R1 exact constitutional signatures mismatched in both domains; Interim correctly persisted for R2. Preferences or conditional offers were never used as signatures.
Uppercase COUNCIL values in JN opening and JS first reply were normalized case-insensitively into Council on mechanical sheets; authored files were unchanged.
R2 already-spent Grey Petrel represented as Keep/no intervention mechanically, with actual spent state preserved.
Mechanical council sheets include standard schema aliases requested by root; no speech or choice changed.
Root independently validated both resolved states and supporting genuine commitments; no arithmetic correction was required.

Late final replies were preserved in contribution files, but not all were delivered before lock. In particular 06_A direct rejection was not returned to JN during that council; JN debrief correctly reports no received reply. This is a delivery limitation, not an invented assent or mechanical correction.
caveats: Asynchronous text packets and bounded exchanges do not reproduce human interruptions, pressure, timing or physical table handling.
No provisional article enacted, so the final NG/MJ duties and delegated powers were not operationally tested within this run.
Players were not given an optimal line or future vision. Favorable hidden Repair+Trade benefit was not selected by A, so final Communities 4 should not be read as entirely planned.
All faction assets survived and both contracts were completed. Distinguish actual reserve expenditure and civilian Raid cost from future duties and preferred constitutional powers never gained.
Readiness 4 to 3 stayed within the printed strong-support band. Neutral questions about practical cost and upkeep were supplied only after votes, per root request.
